design_detail: Retrospective review of New York City Office of Chief Medical Examiner files, 1990–1995, analysed as an ecological comparison of days (filed as retrospective-cohort, the nearest design the schema has: the units are calendar days, each classed as 'hot' or 'other' by the city's daily maximum temperature, and the outcome is the number of deaths certified on that day). Split sample: the 1990–1992 'index sample' (1096 days, 1382 cocaine overdose deaths) and the 10 hyperthermia deaths with benzoylecgonine detected (1990–1995) were used to choose a threshold of 31.1°C (88°F); the threshold was then tested on the 1993–1995 'cross-validation sample' (1095 days; 2008 cocaine overdose deaths). Negative-control outcomes: daily counts of opiate overdose deaths without cocaine (793) and of other overdose deaths (85). Proxy for population cocaine use on each type of day: the share of homicides (4638 tested) and of traffic deaths at ages 15–54 (815 tested) with cocaine in blood.
can_establish: That in New York City in 1993–1995 more deaths per day were certified by the medical examiner as unintentional cocaine overdose on hot days than on other days, while the counts of opiate and other overdose deaths and the share of homicide and traffic victims with cocaine in blood did not differ significantly by type of day.
cannot_establish: That heat raises the risk of death for a person who uses cocaine (nobody's heat exposure, dose or use on the day was known, and there is no count of the people using cocaine each day); by what mechanism (hyperthermia or cardiovascular strain); that the association is specific to cocaine (the cocaine and opiate estimates were never compared directly); or that it is due to temperature rather than to something else that differs between summer days and the rest of the year (no adjustment for season, month, day of week, holidays or trend).

sample.recruitment: Records (registry): all deaths in New York City handled by the Office of Chief Medical Examiner, which assesses every death believed unnatural, identified by manual review of all its medical files for 1990–1995 (pp. 1795–1796, Methods › Fatal Unintentional Drug Overdoses, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: A death entered the overdose series if the medical examiner certified it as an unintentional overdose caused by one or more drugs; overdoses certified as suicide or homicide were excluded (Methods › Fatal Unintentional Drug Overdoses, 1st paragraph, pp. 1795–1796). Certification as death from intoxication required toxicology within the range usually found in such deaths, a history and circumstances consistent with fatal intoxication, and an autopsy without a disease or injury inconsistent with continued life (same section, 2nd paragraph, p. 1796). When several drugs were present above trace amounts, all were customarily listed as the cause, unless one was extremely high and the others at concentrations seen in people dying of other unequivocal causes (3rd paragraph, p. 1796). Deaths were then put into three hierarchical, mutually exclusive groups: (1) cocaine causative, judged from history, circumstances, autopsy and toxicology; (2) opiates causative, with cocaine or its metabolite not detected or detected in clinically insignificant amounts; (3) other substances (4th paragraph, p. 1796). Hyperthermia sample: deaths certified as due to hyperthermia and not classified as unintentional overdoses (n=48), of which those with benzoylecgonine detected at autopsy (n=10) (p. 1796, Methods › Temperature Data, 2nd paragraph). Traffic comparison restricted to ages 15–54 because 95% of cocaine overdoses occur in that range (p. 1796, Comparison Groups).
sample.demographics: Cocaine overdose deaths 1993–1995: mean age 39.0 years (SD 8.8), 94.9% aged 15–54; 1569 men (78.1%) and 439 women (21.9%); 505 non-Hispanic white (25.2%), 884 non-Hispanic Black (44.0%), 605 Hispanic (30.1%), 14 Asian or other (0.6%) (p. 1797). Homicides positive for cocaine: mean age 32.9 (SD 9.0), 97.5% aged 15–54, 83.6% men; traffic deaths positive for cocaine: mean age 34.4 (SD 8.5), 79.5% men (p. 1798). Hyperthermia deaths (n=48): 34 male (70.8%), 14 female (29.2%); 3 infants under 1 year, 29 aged 15–54, 16 over 54 (p. 1797).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (record review). Coverage: complete autopsies in 93% of the 2008 cocaine overdose deaths (p. 1797); cocaine tested in blood in 4638 of 4793 homicides (96.8%) and in 815 of 921 traffic deaths at ages 15–54 (88.5%) (p. 1798); 40 of the 48 hyperthermia deaths (83.3%) screened for benzoylecgonine and cocaine, 41 for ethanol (p. 1797).
sample.selection_effects: Deaths are counted only through medical examiner certification, so the series depends on the examiner's judgment that cocaine caused the death. Deaths certified as hyperthermia were kept out of the overdose series even when benzoylecgonine was found (10 in six years); the authors suggest that some deaths certified as acute cocaine intoxication may have been undetected hyperthermia, because hyperthermia is a clinical diagnosis without pathological findings and people may be found hours after death (p. 1799, Comment, 4th paragraph). The homicide and traffic groups were chosen as proxies for cocaine use in the same population because of similar demographics and neighbourhoods (p. 1796, Comparison Groups); they are not samples of people who use cocaine.

exposure.measurement: Hourly temperatures from the National Weather Service station in Central Park, Manhattan, for every day from 1 January 1990 to 31 December 1995; the exposure is the city-wide daily maximum (p. 1796, Temperature Data). A day was 'hot' if its maximum hourly temperature, or that of the preceding day, was 31.1°C (88°F) or more (a 1-day lag; Methods › Temperature Data, 4th paragraph, pp. 1796–1797; Table 1 footnote, p. 1797). The threshold was chosen from the median maximum temperature on the dates of the 10 hyperthermia deaths with benzoylecgonine detected (30.9°C; range 17.2 to 39.4°C; mean 29.6°C, SD 6.1) and from the index-sample plot, flat to 27.8°C and rising more steeply from 31.1°C (pp. 1796–1797; Figure 1). The heat index correlated with the daily maximum at r=0.986, and analyses using it were said to give similar results, which are not shown (pp. 1797, 1800).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not known. The authors state that the amount of cocaine used before death, the temperature to which people were exposed when they used it, and whether they used occasionally or heavily are all unknown (p. 1800, Comment, 10th paragraph). Route not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Recorded from autopsy toxicology and compared between types of day, not adjusted for. Among cocaine overdose deaths on hot and other days: ethanol 42.9% and 41.4%; opiates 57.1% and 61.7%; benzodiazepines 10.3% and 11.5%; barbiturates 1.2% and 1.4%; salicylates 0.9% and 1.3% (p. 1798). At least one of five drug classes the authors associate with a risk of hyperthermia (antipsychotics, antidepressants, antiparkinsonian and antihistaminic drugs, psychostimulants and sympathomimetics, phencyclidine) was found in 20.3% and 22.0% (Table 2, p. 1798). The 'cocaine overdose' group therefore means deaths in which cocaine was judged causative, with opiates present in most of them; the opiate group excludes deaths with clinically significant cocaine.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (deaths). The timing of the last cocaine use before death is not known.

comparison.controls: Within each overdose group, the 949 'other' days against the 146 hot days of 1993–1995. Negative-control outcomes: daily counts of opiate overdose deaths without cocaine and of other overdose deaths. Proxy for cocaine use in the population: the share of homicides, and of traffic deaths at ages 15–54, with cocaine in blood, on hot against other days.
comparison.matching: None. Cocaine overdose deaths on hot and on other days did not differ significantly by age, race, sex or location of death (p. 1797).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not measured: where people were and what temperature they were exposed to (indoors or outdoors, air conditioning), the amount and pattern of cocaine use, tolerance, heart disease, and the number of people using cocaine on each day. Not modelled: season, month, day of week, holidays, humidity (beyond the unshown heat-index analysis) and trend over the years.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: By definition, the opiate group had no cocaine or only clinically insignificant amounts. The homicide and traffic comparisons concern cocaine in blood only.

outcomes.instruments: Medical examiner certification of cause and manner of death (history, circumstances, autopsy and laboratory data) (p. 1796). Toxicology by the single laboratory of the medical examiner's office on urine and blood taken at autopsy and stored at 4°C: benzoylecgonine screened in urine by enzyme immunoassay (positive at 0.3 mg/L or more) or, without urine, in blood by radioimmunoassay (0.1 mg/L or more), positives substantiated by radioimmunoassay in another tissue; cocaine in blood by gas chromatography with nitrogen–phosphorus detection (0.1 mg/L or more), positives confirmed by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry; opiates by urine enzyme immunoassay or blood radioimmunoassay; ethanol by headspace chromatography; other drugs by several methods (p. 1796, Toxicologic Procedures).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not applicable. The interval between death and autopsy, and between autopsy and assay, is not reported.
outcomes.operationalization: Outcome: the number of deaths per day certified as unintentional overdose in each of the three hierarchical groups; for the comparison groups, the proportion of deaths with cocaine in blood. Hyperthermia deaths: medical examiner certification of hyperthermia as the cause, which the authors note is a clinical diagnosis rather than one established by pathological findings (p. 1799).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; two-tailed alpha of .05 for each of the five tests (three Mann-Whitney comparisons of daily counts, two chi-square tests of proportions) (p. 1797). The differences in Table 2 were not tested.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable to the certification, which was made in routine practice before the study. Whether abstraction from the files was blind to the weather is not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Cross-validation sample 1993–1995 (Table 1, p. 1797): cocaine overdose deaths averaged 2.34 per day on hot days (SD 1.68; 341 deaths on 146 days) and 1.76 on other days (SD 1.37; 1667 deaths on 949 days), Mann-Whitney z=3.98, P<.001, a 33% higher mean. Opiate overdose deaths 0.81 (SD 0.94) and 0.71 (SD 0.86), z=1.08, P=.28. Other overdose deaths 0.08 and 0.08 (SD 0.28 each), z=0.39, P=.69. Share with cocaine in blood: homicides 18.9% (136 of 719) on hot days and 19.5% (766 of 3919) on other days, chi-square 0.11, P=.69; traffic deaths 9.5% (12 of 126) and 10.3% (71 of 689), chi-square 0.01, P=.91 (p. 1798). Editors' calculation from the counts in Table 1 (Poisson rate ratios with 95% intervals; they ignore the overdispersion and the autocorrelation of 0.12 the paper reports, so they are somewhat too narrow): cocaine 1.33 (1.18 to 1.49); opiates 1.14 (0.93 to 1.38); other overdoses 1.07 (0.58 to 1.97); ratio of the cocaine to the opiate rate ratio 1.17 (0.93 to 1.47), P about .18. Difference in mean daily cocaine deaths 0.58 (0.29 to 0.87) (editors' calculation from the printed means and SDs). Editors' calculation of the excess: about 85 more cocaine overdose deaths on the 146 hot days than the other-day rate predicts, about 4% of the 2008 deaths in the three years.
analysis.covariates: None. Unadjusted Mann-Whitney tests with the day as unit, and chi-square tests with the person as unit (p. 1797). Autocorrelation of daily cocaine overdose deaths 0.12 (P<.001); deaths on the previous day accounted for 1.4% of the variance (pp. 1797–1798).
analysis.selective_reporting: Split-sample design: the threshold was chosen on 1990–1992 data and tested once on 1993–1995 data, which guards against choosing the threshold that fits best. The heat-index analyses are described as similar but not shown (p. 1800). The class-by-class percentages of Table 2 are presented without tests, and the text calls the proportions nearly identical although one class differs by about half (5.0% against 9.7%).
analysis.power: Not reported. The 'other overdose' comparison rests on 85 deaths (0.08 a day) and cannot detect even large relative differences (editors' rate-ratio interval 0.58 to 1.97); the opiate comparison cannot exclude an increase of about a third.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In New York City in 1993–1995, days on which that day's or the previous day's maximum reached 31.1°C had a third more deaths certified as unintentional cocaine overdose than other days (2.34 against 1.76 a day). Opiate and other overdose deaths did not differ significantly (0.81 against 0.71; 0.08 against 0.08), and the share of homicide and traffic victims with cocaine in blood was unchanged. Over six years, 10 of the 40 screened deaths certified as hyperthermia had benzoylecgonine detected.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that high ambient temperature is associated with a significant increase in cocaine overdose mortality, that the increase is not explained by changes in cocaine use in the general population, and that cocaine use "appears to be even more dangerous on hot days" (p. 1795). Gaps: (1) the association is between days and death counts; no person's heat exposure or use was known, which the authors acknowledge (p. 1800). (2) The Comment calls the association specific to cocaine (p. 1798), but this rests on non-significant opiate and other-overdose tests, not on a comparison of the estimates; by the editors' calculation the opiate rate ratio is 1.14 (0.93 to 1.38) and does not differ significantly from the cocaine ratio of 1.33. (3) Season and other time-varying factors were not adjusted for. (4) The 'not explained by use' argument rests on homicide and traffic victims as proxies for people using cocaine on each day, and on an unshown statement that screening rates do not change with the weather (p. 1799). (5) The Comment's statement that a quarter of hyperthermia decedents under 55 had used cocaine immediately before death (p. 1798) reads the detection of cocaine as the timing of use, and its comparison with a 1.3% survey prevalence of past-month use (p. 1799) sets a toxicology finding in deaths against self-report in households. Against this, the discussion is restrained: it says the temperature effect has no major influence on annual cocaine mortality, because only about 10% of days reach the threshold (pp. 1798–1799), and that a direct effect cannot be proved (p. 1800).

timeline.event: Editorial on this paper in the same JAMA issue (Kilbourne, 1998, 'Cocaine use and death during heat waves'; cited on p. 1795 as the editorial comment on p. 1828; not among the files read for this card).

Auger et al. (2017), 'Association of elevated ambient temperature with death from cocaine overdose' (Drug and Alcohol Dependence), is on the project's reading list for the same question; not read for this card.

replication.where_it_stands: Provisional: no replication was read for this card. The project's reading list names a later study of the same association (Auger et al., 2017) and population studies of heat and drug deaths or emergency visits (Bohnert et al., 2010; Henderson et al., 2023; Chang et al., 2023), none appraised yet; the status should be set when they are. Within this paper the result was reproduced out of sample, from the 1990–1992 data on which the threshold was chosen to the 1993–1995 data on which it was tested.

funding.funder: Grant DA 06534 from the National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA) and the Dewitt Wallace Reader's Digest Foundation (p. 1800).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the Departments of Psychiatry and of Public Health, Cornell University Medical College; one author (Hirsch) from the Office of Chief Medical Examiner, New York, and the Department of Forensic Medicine, New York University School of Medicine, the office whose certifications are the study's outcome data (p. 1795). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A time-series or case-crossover analysis of cocaine-involved deaths over many years and several cities, with daily temperature and humidity, adjusted for season, day of week, holidays and trend, in which opioid-only deaths are analysed in the same model so that the difference between drugs is tested directly; with scene information (indoors or outdoors, air conditioning) and recorded signs of hyperthermia, to separate a heat effect on people who used cocaine from more use on hot days.

domains.note: No adjustment of any kind: hot days are summer days, and season, month, day of week, holidays and trend were not modelled. The negative-control outcomes (opiate and other overdose deaths; cocaine positivity in homicides and traffic deaths) partly address this, but they are imprecise and were not compared with the cocaine estimate.

One weather station's daily maximum stands for everyone's exposure; nobody's actual temperature (indoors, air conditioning) is known. The threshold was chosen on earlier data, which avoids fitting it to the test data. Misclassification of this kind would mostly weaken an association.
All deaths certified by one city's medical examiner over three years, whatever the weather.
Complete autopsies in 93% of cocaine overdose deaths; cocaine tested in 96.8% of homicides and 88.5% of traffic deaths.

Cause of death is the examiner's judgment from history, circumstances, autopsy and toxicology, not blind to the circumstances of the death; hyperthermia certification, which removed 10 cocaine-positive deaths from the overdose series, depends on findings that may themselves vary with the weather.
One prespecified threshold tested out of sample; all three overdose groups and both comparison groups reported. The heat-index analyses are mentioned but not shown.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The count data are complete medical examiner series, and the split-sample test of a threshold chosen in advance is a real strength. But the comparison of hot with other days is entirely unadjusted, so seasonal factors that travel with heat cannot be excluded, and the comparisons offered against them are too imprecise to show that the association is specific to cocaine. ROBINS-E overall follows the worst domain (confounding). The card may be cited for the higher number of certified cocaine overdose deaths on hot days in New York City in 1993–1995, for how those deaths were defined and tested, and for the other drugs found in them; not for an individual's risk, for a mechanism, or for an effect shown to be specific to cocaine.

key_findings.finding: In 1993–1995 (1095 days, 146 of them hot), New York City had 2008 deaths certified as unintentional cocaine overdose: a mean of 2.34 a day (SD 1.68; 341 deaths) on hot days against 1.76 (SD 1.37; 1667 deaths) on other days, Mann-Whitney z=3.98, P<.001, a 33% higher mean.
key_findings.locator: Results › Fatal Unintentional Cocaine Overdoses, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Table 1
key_findings.note: A 'hot' day is one on which that day's or the previous day's maximum reached 31.1°C (88°F) (Table 1 footnote); the abstract describes hot days without the lag day.

key_findings.finding: Opiate overdose deaths without cocaine: 0.81 a day (SD 0.94; 118 deaths) on hot days against 0.71 (SD 0.86; 675 deaths) on other days, z=1.08, P=.28. Other overdose deaths: 0.08 against 0.08 (12 and 73 deaths), z=0.39, P=.69. The smoothed plots show no visible change with temperature for either group.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 1797); Results › Fatal Unintentional Overdoses of Opiates and Other Drugs (p. 1798); Figures 3 and 4 (p. 1799)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the counts: opiate rate ratio 1.14 (95% CI 0.93 to 1.38) against 1.33 (1.18 to 1.49) for cocaine; the two do not differ significantly (ratio 1.17, 0.93 to 1.47). A null opiate test is not evidence that the association is confined to cocaine.

key_findings.finding: The share of deaths with cocaine in blood did not change with the weather: homicides 18.9% (136 of 719) on hot days and 19.5% (766 of 3919) on other days, P=.69; traffic deaths at ages 15–54, 9.5% (12 of 126) and 10.3% (71 of 689), P=.91.

Cocaine overdose deaths were mostly deaths with other drugs present as well: opiates were detected in 57.1% (hot days) and 61.7% (other days), ethanol in 42.9% and 41.4%, benzodiazepines in 10.3% and 11.5%; at least one of five drug classes the authors link to a risk of hyperthermia in 20.3% and 22.0%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Fatal Unintentional Cocaine Overdoses, 4th and 5th paragraphs; Table 2

key_findings.finding: How a death was counted as a cocaine overdose: the medical examiner certified an unintentional overdose by one or more drugs (toxicology in the range usual in such deaths, consistent history and circumstances, no disease or injury inconsistent with life at autopsy); the authors then classed it as cocaine-caused when cocaine was judged causative from history, circumstances, autopsy and toxicology, ahead of opiates and other drugs in a hierarchy. Complete autopsies were done in 93% of the 2008 deaths.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Fatal Unintentional Drug Overdoses, 1st paragraph (pp. 1795–1796) to 4th paragraph (p. 1796); Results › Fatal Unintentional Cocaine Overdoses, 2nd paragraph (p. 1797)

key_findings.finding: Toxicology was done in one laboratory on autopsy urine and blood stored at 4°C: benzoylecgonine by urine immunoassay (positive at 0.3 mg/L or more) or blood radioimmunoassay (0.1 mg/L or more), confirmed in another tissue; cocaine in blood by gas chromatography (0.1 mg/L or more), confirmed by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry.

Of 48 deaths certified as hyperthermia in 1990–1995 (not classed as overdoses), 40 were screened: benzoylecgonine was detected in 10 (25% of those screened, 21% of all 48) and cocaine in 7; opiates in 1 of 40 and ethanol in 5 of 41. Restricted to ages 15–54 (n=27), 37.0% had benzoylecgonine and 25.9% cocaine.
key_findings.locator: Results › Deaths Due to Hyperthermia, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: The same section gives 29 deaths aged 15–54 (60.4%); the denominator of 27 is not explained (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: The threshold of 31.1°C (88°F) was chosen from the median daily maximum on the dates of the 10 hyperthermia deaths with benzoylecgonine (30.9°C; range 17.2 to 39.4°C) and from the 1990–1992 index sample (1096 days, 1382 cocaine overdose deaths), in which the cumulative mean of deaths was flat up to 27.8°C and rose more steeply from 31.1°C.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Temperature Data, 2nd to 4th paragraphs (the 4th continuing on p. 1797); Figure 1 (p. 1797)

key_findings.finding: Daily cocaine overdose deaths were autocorrelated at 0.12 (P<.001); deaths on the previous day accounted for 1.4% of the variance. Decedents on hot and on other days did not differ significantly by age, race, sex or location of death. The two days with the most cocaine overdose deaths (printed as n=9) had maxima of 37.2°C and 33.3°C.
key_findings.locator: Results › Fatal Unintentional Cocaine Overdoses, 3rd paragraph (p. 1797, continuing on p. 1798)

key_findings.finding: The authors state that only about 10% of days in a year reach 31.1°C in New York City, so the temperature effect does not have a major influence on annual cocaine overdose mortality.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from Table 1: about 85 deaths above the other-day rate on the 146 hot days, some 4% of the 2008 deaths of 1993–1995.

key_findings.finding: The authors suggest that some deaths certified as acute cocaine intoxication may have been undetected hyperthermia, because hyperthermia is a clinical diagnosis without pathological findings and people who die after using cocaine may not be found for hours.

Limitations stated by the authors: the dose used before death, the temperature at the time of use, and whether people used occasionally or heavily are unknown; the threshold applies to a group, not to individuals, and may differ in other cities.

reporting_issues.issue: The hyperthermia section reports 29 deaths aged 15–54 (60.4% of 48), but the analysis restricted to that age group uses n=27, with 37.0% (10) positive for benzoylecgonine and 25.9% (7) for cocaine; the difference is not explained (it may be the number screened).
reporting_issues.consequence: The Comment's 'a quarter of all individuals younger than 55' (p. 1798) rests on 7 of 27, a denominator that excludes the three infants under 1 year and possibly two unscreened deaths.

reporting_issues.issue: The Comment says at least 1 in 4 deaths known to result from hyperthermia had a positive cocaine test (p. 1799), but 1 in 4 is the share of the 40 screened deaths (10); of all 48 the known minimum is 10 (21%), as the Results state (p. 1797).
reporting_issues.consequence: The lower bound is about 1 in 5, not 1 in 4; cite 10 of 40 screened (25%) or 10 of 48 (21%).

reporting_issues.issue: For homicides, the printed chi-square of 0.11 with 1 df corresponds to P of about .74, not the printed .69; recomputed from the printed counts, the uncorrected chi-square is about 0.15 (P about .69) and the continuity-corrected value about 0.12 (P about .73). The traffic result (chi-square 0.01, P=.91) matches a continuity-corrected test (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: None for the conclusion (no difference either way), but the statistic and its P value come from different versions of the test.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract defines hot days as days with a maximum of 31.1°C or more, whereas the analysis also counts the day after such a day as hot (1-day lag; p. 1797, Methods and Table 1 footnote).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 33% difference applies to days that were hot or followed a hot day; a claim should use the paper's own definition.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Comment say cocaine overdose deaths increased steadily above the threshold, but this is read from a cumulative mean curve (Figure 1) and from 5-degree moving averages (Figure 2), whose highest-temperature points rest on few days and which do not rise smoothly; no test of trend is reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper supports a higher mean above the threshold, not a demonstrated dose–response above it.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the proportion of cocaine overdose deaths positive for drugs associated with hyperthermia was nearly identical on hot and other days (p. 1798); this holds for 'any drug' (20.3% against 22.0%), but antiparkinsonian and antihistaminic drugs were found in 5.0% against 9.7%. No class was tested.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the class differences cannot be interpreted without tests.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that drug screening rates are not influenced by hot weather in New York City is given without data.
reporting_issues.consequence: The argument from the comparison groups that cocaine use did not rise on hot days depends on this unshown premise.

reporting_issues.issue: The legend of Figure 4 gives the period as 1992 through 1995, whereas the cross-validation period, and the legends of Figures 2 and 3, are 1993 through 1995. The opiate cut-off in blood is printed as '0.1 mg' without a volume (p. 1796).
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; no effect on the results.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), JAMA 279(22), pp. 1795–1800 (all pages; Tables 1–2 and Figures 1–4 checked on rendered pages; figure values not extracted beyond what the text states; no supplement). The editorial comment named on p. 1795 (Kilbourne, 1998, 10.1001/jama.279.22.1828) was not among the files read.
